Patients with localized prostate cancer generally prefer lower radiation doses over more aggressive treatment, as they prioritize quality-of-life aspects such as reducing gastrointestinal (GI) toxicity compared to improving survival rates. A study suggests that patients with fewer than 5 metastatic sites had better long-term survival, indicating early detection and treatment of a small number of metastases may be beneficial for improving outcomes. Currently available nomograms predicting biochemical recurrence (BCR) accurately forecast both prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels and other clinically relevant endpoints, such as post-chemotherapy PSA-free survival. However, adjusting PSA for body mass index does not appear to significantly impact accuracy in predicting clinical outcomes.

While some patients with localized prostate cancer do prefer more aggressive treatment due to improved survival rates, the majority of patients prioritize quality-of-life aspects over short-term survival gains. Treatment preferences and patient values should be incorporated into radiotherapy decision-making to ensure that patients' needs are adequately addressed.

It is essential to consider individual patient characteristics, such as overall health, tumor biology, and side effects tolerance, when making treatment decisions for localized prostate cancer. Patients with a smaller number of metastatic sites may benefit from early detection and aggressive treatment to improve long-term survival outcomes.
